sources.title: Dash Academy curriculum — module 1 manifest row

claims.text: A block chain is a chain of blocks in which each block references the block before it; each block stores the hash of the previous block's header and a merkle root of its own transactions, so a transaction cannot be modified without modifying its block and every block after it.
The block chain is Dash's public ledger: an ordered, timestamped record of transactions whose purpose is to protect against double spending and against modification of earlier transaction records.
Each full node independently stores a chain of blocks it has itself validated against the consensus rules; nodes holding the same validated blocks are said to be in consensus.

Value does not move wallet-to-wallet as a stored balance; it moves from the output of one transaction to the input of the next. Each output may be spent only once, so a second attempt to spend it is a forbidden double spend.
A wallet balance is really the total duffs held in one or more unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs). A transaction is valid only if its inputs are unspent outputs.
Dash value is denominated in duffs; one dash equals 100,000,000 duffs.

A private key is 256 bits of secret random data. A public key is derived from it using ECDSA on the secp256k1 curve; the public key is hashed to a 20-byte pubkey hash, which is encoded as a Dash address using base58check (a version number, the hash, and a checksum to catch typos).

Spending a standard P2PKH output requires a signature script holding the full public key and an ECDSA signature; the output's pubkey script checks that the supplied public key hashes to the expected value and that the signature was made with the matching private key.

The signature covers the whole transaction except the signature scripts, making it tamper-proof so it can be broadcast over the peer-to-peer network; every peer and miner validates it independently before relaying or including it.

Because the ledger is replicated across many independently validating nodes with no central controller, no single server can be shut down, censored, or silently rewrite history — which is what 'decentralized' buys an application as opposed to a database one company owns.
A wallet program creates public keys to receive duffs and uses the corresponding private keys to spend them; a wallet file stores the private keys.
Reusing a public key or address lets others track a person's receiving and spending; using a fresh key for each receive and spend improves privacy and security.

uncertainties.topic: The core docs describe consensus and independent validation but never state verbatim why decentralization matters to an app developer.
uncertainties.resolution: Derive it as an inference from the node/consensus/ledger sources, kept strictly effects-focused (no masternodes, no second tier): no single server to shut down, censor, or silently rewrite records, and the network itself is the backend. Labeled 'inference' in claim C10.

uncertainties.topic: Whether 'what a blockchain is' should mention how new blocks get proposed (mining/proof of work).
uncertainties.resolution: Name the effect only in one sentence (computers compete to propose the next block and are rewarded for the one the network accepts), via the existing <Term id="mining"> glossary term, and defer all proof-of-work machinery.

uncertainties.topic: Whether to teach only the classic base58check payment address or also Platform's bech32m addresses.
uncertainties.resolution: Teach only the classic base58check payment address as the standard payment-address form in this lesson; leave Platform's bech32m addresses to module 8.

uncertainties.topic: Which incidental terms need new glossary entries versus inline definition.
uncertainties.resolution: Define transaction, key, private key, public key, and address in prose (they are mustCover and belong to the lesson). Use <Term> with new glossary entries only for incidental jargon: consensus and secp256k1.
